title: Reception, Admission, Referral and Discharge Procedures
path: Reception, Admission, Referral and Discharge Procedures

headings.title: Ward Reception and Orientation
headings.content:
The way a patient is welcomed into a hospital ward shapes their entire experience and emotional state. Ward reception begins the moment a patient crosses the threshold of the nursing unit. A warm, calm greeting helps reduce the anxiety typical of hospital admissions. 

- **Immediate Greeting**: Acknowledge the patient and their relatives promptly by name with a reassuring tone.
- **Physical Environment**: Introduce the patient to their bed space, locker, call bell, and toilet facilities.
- **Personnel Introduction**: Present key staff members, including the ward manager, primary nurse, and attending doctors.
- **Ward Routine**: Explain meal times, visiting hours, and safety regulations simply.

headings.title: Procedures of Hospital Admission
headings.content:
Hospital admission is the official acceptance of a patient to occupy a bed in the ward for diagnosis, treatment, and nursing care. Admissions generally fall into two categories: emergency and elective.

- **Emergency Admission**: Unplanned entry due to sudden illness, severe trauma, or acute crisis. Life-saving measures take precedence over paperwork.
- **Elective Admission**: Planned entry scheduled in advance for non-urgent investigations, chronic disease workups, or scheduled surgeries.

Upon arrival, the nurse assesses vital signs, checks the admission notes from the clinic or emergency room, and settles the patient comfortably.

headings.title: Documentation and Record Keeping During Admission
headings.content:
Accurate documentation during admission forms the legal and clinical foundation of the patient's hospital stay. The nurse compiles several standardized forms to track clinical status and care plans. 

The admission package typically includes the admission register, the master index card, the doctor's order sheet, and the initial nursing assessment sheet. The nurse must record baseline vital signs, known allergies, current medications, and a thorough inventory of personal belongings brought into the ward. Missing valuables or inaccurate allergy records pose serious legal and safety hazards.

headings.title: Patient Referral Principles and Procedures
headings.content:
Referral is the process of sending a patient from one health care level or facility to another for specialized management that is unavailable at the current facility. Effective referral requires seamless communication between healthcare providers.

The referral process follows a clear chain: stabilization of the patient, completion of a formal referral letter detailing findings and treatment given, arrangement of appropriate transport, and accompaniment by a skilled nurse or doctor when the condition is unstable. A poorly managed referral often leads to delayed treatment and increased mortality.

headings.title: Inter-Facility and Intra-Facility Transfer Guidelines
headings.content:
Moving a patient within the same hospital is an intra-facility transfer, while moving them to another distinct hospital is an inter-facility transfer. Both require careful planning to maintain continuity of care.

- **Intra-Facility Transfer**: Moving from the emergency room to the intensive care unit, or from surgery back to the general ward. Requires updating bed census and handing over notes.
- **Inter-Facility Transfer**: Requires stabilization, ambulance coordination, informed consent from the family, and a formal verbal handover between the sending and receiving nurse.

headings.title: Discharge Planning and Preparation
headings.content:
Discharge planning is a continuous, coordinated process that starts right from the day of admission. It ensures the patient transitions safely from the hospital back to their home or another care facility.

Effective planning involves assessing the home environment, evaluating family support, organizing necessary medications, and arranging follow-up clinic appointments. Nurses must educate the patient and caregivers on wound care, warning signs of complications, and dietary restrictions before they leave the ward.

headings.title: Types of Discharge and Nursing Responsibilities
headings.content:
Patients leave the hospital under various circumstances, each carrying specific nursing responsibilities and documentation requirements.

- **Routine Discharge**: Planned release authorized by the doctor when treatment goals are met.
- **Discharge Against Medical Advice (AMA)**: A patient chooses to leave voluntarily against professional medical counsel. The nurse must inform the doctor, explain potential risks, and have the patient sign an AMA form.
- **Absconding**: A patient leaves the hospital premises secretly without notifying staff. Nurses must report this immediately to hospital security and administration.
- **Death**: Pronouncement of death by a doctor followed by last offices and morgue transfer.
